title: SDS Split & the Weatherman Faction
body:
In June 1969, at the Students for a Democratic Society convention in Chicago, a militant faction seized control of the organization and issued a manifesto titled "You Don't Need a Weatherman to Know Which Way the Wind Blows," borrowing a line from Bob Dylan. Calling themselves the Weathermen, they argued that the time for mass student protest had passed and that revolutionaries inside the imperialist United States had a duty to take direct, militant action in solidarity with Black liberation and Third World anti-colonial struggles.

The Weatherman takeover effectively destroyed SDS, the largest organization of the 1960s New Left, splitting it into warring factions. Rejecting the patient organizing of the student movement, the Weathermen set out to "bring the war home" — to make the cost of the Vietnam War felt inside the United States.

title: Days of Rage
body:
In October 1969 the Weathermen staged the "Days of Rage" in Chicago, a series of confrontational demonstrations timed to the trial of the Chicago Eight. Expecting thousands, they drew only a few hundred, who charged through the streets of the Gold Coast smashing windows and battling police.

The action left many arrested and injured and alienated much of the broader movement, which saw it as reckless adventurism. But for the Weathermen it marked a decisive break from mass, nonviolent student organizing and set the group on the path toward clandestine armed struggle.

title: Haymarket Police Monument Bombing
body:
In early October 1969, days before the Days of Rage, the Weathermen bombed the Haymarket Police Monument in Chicago — a statue commemorating the police killed in the 1886 Haymarket affair and long a symbol of the conflict between labor and the police. The blast destroyed the statue.

It was one of the group's earliest symbolic bombings, deliberately targeting a monument that represented state power over radical movements. The statue was rebuilt and bombed again by the Weathermen the following year before being moved to a secure location.

title: Greenwich Village Townhouse Explosion
body:
On March 6, 1970, a bomb under construction detonated accidentally in a townhouse on West 11th Street in Greenwich Village, killing three Weather members — Diana Oughton, Ted Gold, and Terry Robbins. The group had been building an antipersonnel bomb reportedly intended for a soldiers' dance at Fort Dix, New Jersey.

The disaster was a turning point. Shocked by the deaths and by how close they had come to a massacre, the survivors reconstituted the group as the Weather Underground, renounced attacks aimed at killing people, and adopted a policy of bombing property — with advance warnings — rather than taking lives. The explosion drove the group fully underground.

title: New York Police Headquarters Bombing
body:
On June 9, 1970, the Weather Underground bombed the New York City Police Headquarters, one of its first actions under the new, property-focused strategy adopted after the townhouse disaster. As would become the group's practice, a warning was phoned in beforehand and the building was evacuated; the blast caused damage but no deaths.

The bombing announced that the group had survived the townhouse catastrophe and would continue its campaign against symbols of state power — police, courts, and the military — while trying to avoid casualties.

title: Timothy Leary Prison Escape
body:
In September 1970 the Weather Underground helped the imprisoned LSD guru Timothy Leary escape from the California Men's Colony, where he was serving time on marijuana charges. Members smuggled him out and spirited him abroad; he ultimately reached Algeria, where Eldridge Cleaver's Black Panther International Section was based.

The escape, financed in part by a countercultural drug network, demonstrated the Weather Underground's links to the wider counterculture and its capacity for clandestine operations. Leary issued a militant communiqué on his release, though he and the Panthers soon fell out.

title: U.S. Capitol Bombing
body:
On March 1, 1971, the Weather Underground detonated a bomb inside the United States Capitol, in a restroom near the Senate chamber, to protest the U.S.-backed invasion of Laos. A warning was phoned in beforehand and the building was cleared; the blast caused significant damage but no injuries.

Bombing the Capitol itself was among the group's most audacious acts, striking at the very seat of the government prosecuting the war. It drew national attention and cemented the Weather Underground's reputation as the era's most prominent white radical underground.

title: Pentagon Bombing
body:
On May 19, 1972 — a date chosen to mark the birthday of Ho Chi Minh — the Weather Underground bombed the Pentagon, planting a device in a fourth-floor restroom in protest of the renewed U.S. bombing of North Vietnam. As usual a warning preceded the blast, which flooded part of the building but caused no casualties.

Bombing the headquarters of the U.S. military was a high point of the group's campaign against the Vietnam War, and it embarrassed the government by exposing the vulnerability of even its most secure buildings.

title: Prairie Fire Manifesto
body:
In 1974 the Weather Underground published Prairie Fire: The Politics of Revolutionary Anti-Imperialism, a book-length manifesto distributed clandestinely across the country. Named for Mao Zedong's line that "a single spark can start a prairie fire," it laid out the group's revolutionary program and sought to reconnect the isolated underground with aboveground mass movements.

Prairie Fire marked a strategic shift toward rebuilding a broader political base and inspired the aboveground Prairie Fire Organizing Committee. It reflected a growing recognition within the group that clandestine bombings alone could not build a revolution.

title: State Department Bombing
body:
On January 29, 1975, the Weather Underground bombed the U.S. State Department building in Washington, D.C., again in protest of U.S. policy in Southeast Asia. Consistent with the group's practice, a warning was issued and the explosion caused damage but no injuries.

It was one of the group's last major bombings. By this point the Vietnam War was ending, the movement that had sustained the underground was fading, and internal divisions were mounting.

title: Surrenders & Decline
body:
In the late 1970s the Weather Underground disintegrated amid the end of the Vietnam War, internal splits over strategy (the "Hard Times" conflict), and the collapse of the movement around it. Beginning in 1977 and continuing into the 1980s, many members surfaced and turned themselves in.

Most faced surprisingly light consequences or saw charges dropped, because the government's case had been built on illegal surveillance, break-ins, and wiretaps carried out under the FBI's COINTELPRO program — abuses that were themselves later exposed and prosecuted. A few members, however, continued into other clandestine formations and were later imprisoned for actions such as the 1981 Brink's robbery.
